title: Diagnose CloudFront 403 Error
description: A user reports receiving a 403 Access Denied error when accessing static assets through CloudFront. Inspect the architecture to find the root cause.

answers.text: Route53 DNS misconfiguration
CloudFront cache corruption
S3 bucket policy blocking CloudFront
TLS handshake failure

explanation: The S3 bucket policy is missing. When using CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC), the S3 bucket must have a policy that explicitly grants s3:GetObject permission to the CloudFront service principal. Without this policy, S3 denies all requests from CloudFront, resulting in a 403 Access Denied error.

title: Diagnose S3 Access Issue
description: A user cannot download an object from an S3 bucket. Use the AWS CLI simulator to investigate and identify the root cause.
scenario: A developer at a partner company (AWS account 987654321098) reports they cannot download objects from the `my-app-bucket` S3 bucket in your account (111122223333). They receive an AccessDenied error despite having AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess attached to their user. Use the simulated AWS CLI to investigate and determine the root cause.

commands.output: An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListObjectsV2 operation: Access Denied
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListObjectsV2 operation: Access Denied
An error occurred (AWSOrganizationsNotInUseException) when calling the DescribeOrganization operation: Your account is not a member of an organization.

commands.command: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::987654321098:user/dev-user --action-names s3:GetObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/report.csv

answers.text: The IAM user does not have an S3 policy attached
The bucket policy denies access to principals outside the AWS Organisation
The bucket's KMS encryption key denies access to external accounts
Block Public Access is preventing the partner account from reading objects

explanation:
The bucket policy contains an explicit Deny with a StringNotEquals condition on aws:PrincipalOrgID. Any principal whose account is NOT in organisation o-abc123def4 is denied all s3:* actions.

The developer's account (987654321098) is not a member of that organisation - confirmed by the DescribeOrganization error.

In AWS IAM, an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow, so AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess is irrelevant. The fix is to add the partner account or role as an exception in the bucket policy.

title: Fix S3 IAM Policy
description: An EC2 instance role cannot correctly access an S3 bucket. Fix the IAM policy to grant the correct least-privilege access.
scenario: An EC2 instance needs to list objects in `my-app-bucket`, read objects, and upload new objects. The current policy is broken: it grants overly broad access on the wrong resource and is missing required permissions. Fix the policy to follow least-privilege principles.
explanation:
Three issues needed fixing:

1. Resource was arn:aws:s3:::* - far too broad. Object operations require the objects ARN arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/*.
2. s3:PutObject was missing - the role needs to upload, not just read.
3. s3:ListBucket was missing and requires the bucket ARN (no /*) as the Resource - a common mistake is using the objects ARN for ListBucket, which silently fails.

The correct policy has two statements: one for object operations on the /* ARN, and one for ListBucket on the bare bucket ARN.

title: Build a Highly Available Web Application
description: Design a fault-tolerant web application architecture using AWS services. Place the correct components and connect them properly.
scenario: Your company is launching a customer-facing web application that must remain available 24/7 and tolerate any single component or AZ failure. The platform team mandates an RTO under 5 minutes. Design the architecture from the available components.
validationChecks: ALB routes to EC2 instances in multiple AZs
EC2 instances connect to RDS Primary
RDS Primary has a Multi-AZ standby for automatic failover
EC2 instances connect to S3 and route outbound traffic via NAT Gateway
explanation:
A fault-tolerant architecture needs:

- CloudFront for edge caching and latency reduction
- ALB distributing traffic across two AZs so the app survives any single AZ failure
- EC2 in both AZs
- S3 for durable static-asset storage
- NAT Gateway for private-subnet outbound access
- RDS Primary for transactional data
- RDS Standby (Multi-AZ) for synchronous replication and automatic failover in under 60 seconds

The five decoys - ElastiCache, WAF, Route 53, Secrets Manager, ECS Fargate, SQS - serve legitimate production purposes but are not required by the stated HA constraints.

title: Find the Lambda Timeout Root Cause
description: Analyze CloudWatch logs to diagnose why a Lambda function is timing out intermittently.
scenario: Two Lambda functions share the same DynamoDB tables. The OrderProcessor function is intermittently timing out after 30 seconds. Analyze the interleaved CloudWatch logs from both functions to find the root cause of the timeouts.

logs.message: Attaching network interface — waiting for VPC ENI

answers.text: VPC cold start latency is causing OrderProcessor to time out
Token validation is taking too long
DynamoDB table is throttling reads, exhausting Lambda retry budget
A slow DynamoDB query (1847ms) is accumulating to cause the timeout

explanation:
The logs show DDB:PROV_THROUGHPUT_EXCEEDED errors from the OrderProcessor function with exponential backoff retries. The SDK retries consume the entire 30-second Lambda timeout.

Two red herrings to discard:
- VPC ENI cold start (4.2s) belongs to UserRecommendationFunction - it completes successfully
- Slow 1847ms query at 10:07 - the request still completes in 3.2s, well within the timeout

The fix is to switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode or increase provisioned read capacity units.

title: Debug a Failed API Request
description: Trace a failing HTTPS request through the network path from client to API server to find the broken hop.
scenario: Users report 504 Gateway Timeout errors when calling your API at api.example.com. Trace each hop to find where the request fails.

steps.label: DNS Resolution
steps.detail: Route 53 resolves api.example.com to ALB DNS name correctly.

steps.label: TLS Handshake
steps.detail: ACM certificate is valid. TLS 1.2 handshake succeeds.

steps.label: ALB Security Group
steps.detail: ALB security group allows inbound HTTPS (443) from 0.0.0.0/0.

steps.label: Network ACL
steps.detail: Subnet NACL allows all required inbound and outbound traffic.

steps.label: Application
steps.detail: Application is running and healthy on port 8080.

answers.text: Route 53 DNS record is misconfigured
SSL certificate has expired
EC2 security group blocks ALB traffic on port 8080
Application process has crashed

explanation:
The EC2 security group allows inbound traffic on port 80, but the ALB target group forwards to port 8080. Since the security group doesn't allow port 8080, the ALB health checks fail and requests time out with 504 errors.

The fix is to update the EC2 security group to allow inbound traffic on port 8080 from the ALB security group.

title: Order the Incident Response Steps
description: A security incident has been detected. Put the AWS incident response steps in the correct order.
scenario: GuardDuty has detected unauthorized API calls from compromised IAM credentials. Order the incident response steps correctly.

steps.text: Disable the compromised IAM access keys
Attach a deny-all policy to the compromised user
Notify the security team and relevant stakeholders
Review GuardDuty findings for signs of lateral movement
Review CloudTrail logs for the scope of unauthorized activity
Isolate affected EC2 instances and revoke active console sessions
Identify and revert any unauthorized changes to resources
Rotate all credentials and issue new access keys
Document findings and update security policies

explanation:
The correct order:

1. Disable the compromised keys immediately - this is the fastest containment.
2. Apply deny-all to catch any active sessions still using the principal.
3. Notify stakeholders before deep investigation so they are aware.
4. Check GuardDuty for lateral movement signals first - it provides a broader threat picture.
5. Deep dive into CloudTrail for the full action scope.
6. Isolate affected EC2 instances once you understand what was accessed.
7. Revert unauthorized changes.
8. Issue fresh credentials once containment is confirmed.
9. Document and improve policies last.

title: Fix ALB Health Check Configuration
description: An ALB is marking all targets as unhealthy. Fix the health check configuration to restore traffic flow.
scenario: Your ALB target group shows all EC2 targets as unhealthy. The backend service runs without TLS and exposes a dedicated health endpoint. Review the target group health check configuration and correct it to restore target registration.

configItems.label: Health Check Protocol
options: HTTP
HTTPS
TCP
GRPC

explanation:
Four settings need fixing:

1. Protocol must be HTTP - the backend does not terminate TLS.
2. Port must match the application's listening port, not the default 80.
3. Path must match the actual health endpoint, not a generic /health.
4. Healthy Threshold of 5 means a target needs 5 consecutive passes before it's considered healthy - 2 is the AWS recommended minimum for faster recovery.

Response codes should be 200-299 to accept any success code, not just 200. Deregistration delay of 300s is too long for rapid failover; 60s is appropriate for most APIs.

title: Reduce Monthly AWS Spending
description: Optimize an over-provisioned architecture to bring monthly costs under the target budget while maintaining functionality.
scenario: Your team's monthly AWS bill is $2,850. The target budget is $600. Replace over-provisioned services with cost-effective alternatives while maintaining equivalent functionality.

components.name: CloudWatch Logs

alternatives.service: Export to S3 + query with Athena ($40/mo)

components.correctService: Export to S3 + query with Athena ($40/mo)

explanation:
The optimal strategy brings costs to ~$615/mo:

1. Lambda replaces always-on EC2 for variable API traffic ($45 vs $520).
2. Aurora Serverless v2 scales to demand instead of a fixed oversized RDS ($350 vs $1200).
3. VPC Endpoints eliminate NAT data fees for AWS service traffic ($20 vs $210).
4. S3 Lifecycle moves aging objects to cheaper tiers automatically ($65 vs $220).
5. Exporting CloudWatch logs to S3 and querying with Athena is far cheaper than high-volume log ingestion ($40 vs $320).
6. Fargate Spot is suitable for interruptible batch workers - EC2 Spot is cheaper still but requires managing instances ($95 vs $380).

Avoid disabling logging (breaks audit trail) and avoid pure Spot for latency-sensitive APIs.

title: Secure an S3-Backed Application
description: Identify and fix security vulnerabilities in an application that stores user data in S3.
scenario: A security audit of your S3-backed application has identified several vulnerabilities. For each issue, select the correct remediation.

issues.issue: Block Public Access is disabled and bucket ACL grants public read
options: Enable S3 Block Public Access (all settings) and remove public ACL grants
Add a bucket policy denying anonymous access
Enable versioning on the bucket
Move bucket to a private VPC endpoint
issues.correctOption: Enable S3 Block Public Access (all settings) and remove public ACL grants

issues.issue: Server-side encryption is not enabled. Objects are stored unencrypted.
options: Enable SSE-S3 (AES-256) as default encryption
Enable SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key and deny unencrypted uploads via bucket policy
Encrypt objects client-side before upload
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
issues.correctOption: Enable SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key and deny unencrypted uploads via bucket policy

issues.issue: Role policy grants s3:* on Resource: * for the entire account
options: Restrict actions to s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject on the specific bucket ARN only
Add a condition key restricting to the current VPC
Add MFA requirement to the policy
Create a service control policy (SCP) to restrict S3 access
issues.correctOption: Restrict actions to s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject on the specific bucket ARN only

issues.issue: No access logging is enabled. Cannot audit who accessed data.
options: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for the bucket
Enable S3 server access logging to a separate log bucket
Use Amazon Macie to scan for access patterns
Enable VPC Flow Logs
issues.correctOption: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for the bucket

issues.issue: Versioning is disabled. Accidental deletes or overwrites cannot be recovered.
options: Enable versioning with lifecycle rules for non-current versions
Enable cross-region replication
Take daily snapshots using AWS Backup
Enable MFA Delete on the bucket
issues.correctOption: Enable versioning with lifecycle rules for non-current versions

issues.issue: Versioning is enabled but MFA Delete is not configured. Any authenticated user with s3:DeleteObjectVersion can permanently remove object versions.
options: Enable MFA Delete; require MFA for s3:DeleteObjectVersion and s3:PutBucketVersioning
Apply a bucket policy denying delete operations from all principals
Enable Object Lock in GOVERNANCE mode
Restrict DeleteObject permissions via IAM permission boundary
issues.correctOption: Enable MFA Delete; require MFA for s3:DeleteObjectVersion and s3:PutBucketVersioning

issues.issue: Compliance policy requires immutable retention of user records for 7 years. Bucket has Object Lock enabled but retention period is set to 365 days in GOVERNANCE mode.
options: Change Object Lock mode to COMPLIANCE and set retention period to 2,555 days (7 years)
Enable cross-region replication to a second region as a backup
Use S3 Glacier Vault Lock with a 7-year policy instead
Apply a lifecycle rule moving objects to S3 Glacier after 1 year
issues.correctOption: Change Object Lock mode to COMPLIANCE and set retention period to 2,555 days (7 years)

explanation:
The seven critical fixes are:

1. Block Public Access prevents accidental exposure.
2. SSE-KMS with a CMK provides encryption plus audit trail, with a deny policy blocking unencrypted uploads.
3. Least-privilege IAM restricts the role to needed actions on the specific bucket.
4. CloudTrail S3 data events provide per-object audit logging.
5. Versioning with lifecycle rules protects against accidental deletes.
6. MFA Delete adds a second authentication factor to prevent permanent version deletion by compromised credentials.
7. Switching Object Lock to COMPLIANCE mode for 7 years makes retention tamper-proof - even the root account cannot shorten it, satisfying regulatory requirements.

title: Improve API Response Times
description: Optimize a slow serverless API by selecting the correct performance improvement for each bottleneck.
scenario: Your serverless API (API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB) has a P99 latency of 4.2 seconds. The SLA requires P99 under 500ms. Identify the correct optimization for each performance bottleneck.
architectureDescription: Client → CloudFront (not configured) → API Gateway (REST) → Lambda (1024MB, Python 3.12, no provisioned concurrency) → DynamoDB (on-demand, no caching layer)

problems.problem: First invocation after idle period takes 3-5 seconds due to Python runtime initialization and large deployment package (250MB with ML dependencies).
options: Enable Provisioned Concurrency with at least 5 instances
Increase Lambda memory to 3008MB
Switch to Python 3.13 runtime
Reduce Lambda timeout to 5 seconds
problems.correctOption: Enable Provisioned Concurrency with at least 5 instances

problems.problem: Repeated reads for popular items hit DynamoDB directly every time. Average read latency is 8ms but contributes to aggregate latency under load.
options: Switch to DynamoDB strongly consistent reads
Add DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) cluster for microsecond caching
Increase DynamoDB read capacity units
Enable DynamoDB global tables
problems.correctOption: Add DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) cluster for microsecond caching

problems.problem: Identical API responses are generated from scratch on every request. Many endpoints return the same data for minutes at a time.
options: Enable API Gateway response caching with appropriate TTL
Switch from REST API to HTTP API
Add a CloudFront distribution in front of API Gateway
Implement Lambda response streaming
problems.correctOption: Enable API Gateway response caching with appropriate TTL

problems.problem: API returns full DynamoDB item attributes even when clients only need 3-4 fields. Average response is 45KB.
options: Enable API Gateway response compression
Use DynamoDB projection expressions and return only needed fields
Switch to DynamoDB Streams for real-time updates
Paginate all responses to 10 items
problems.correctOption: Use DynamoDB projection expressions and return only needed fields

problems.problem: The Lambda function calls Secrets Manager GetSecretValue on every invocation to retrieve database credentials. Each call adds ~80ms of latency and contributes significant cost at scale.
options: Use the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension with a local cache (TTL 5 min)
Hard-code the database credentials in the Lambda environment variables
Store secrets in S3 and read them at cold start only
Switch to IAM database authentication to eliminate secrets entirely for this use case
problems.correctOption: Use the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension with a local cache (TTL 5 min)

problems.problem: API Gateway execution logging is set to INFO level on all stages and routes, writing a log entry for every request, response, and Lambda integration event. Under load this adds measurable per-request overhead and inflates CloudWatch costs.
options: Set execution logging level to ERROR only in production; use access logging for request tracing
Disable CloudWatch logging entirely to eliminate overhead
Switch to HTTP API which does not support execution logging
Move all APIs to a private VPC endpoint to reduce logging volume
problems.correctOption: Set execution logging level to ERROR only in production; use access logging for request tracing

explanation:
Six optimizations bring latency under 500ms:

1. Provisioned Concurrency eliminates cold starts - the #1 contributor for functions with large packages.
2. DAX provides microsecond caching for hot DynamoDB items.
3. API Gateway caching eliminates Lambda invocations for repeated requests.
4. Projection expressions reduce payload size and data transfer.
5. The Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension caches secrets in the Lambda execution environment, removing the per-invocation Secrets Manager call (~80ms savings).
6. Reducing execution logging to ERROR only removes per-request log overhead; access logs are sufficient for tracing in production.

title: Write a Cross-Account S3 Versioned Access Policy
description: Write an IAM policy that grants read-only access to a specific S3 bucket from a cross-account role.
scenario: Account B (444455556666) needs to read current and historical (versioned) objects from the 'shared-data-bucket' in Account A (111122223333), but must not be able to enumerate other buckets or perform write/delete operations. Write an IAM policy for the Account B role that follows strict least-privilege.
requirements: Allow s3:GetObject on objects in shared-data-bucket only
Allow s3:ListBucket on the shared-data-bucket only
Allow s3:GetObjectVersion on versioned objects in shared-data-bucket only
Deny s3:ListAllMyBuckets — cross-account bucket enumeration must not be permitted
Deny access to any other bucket

testCases.description: Get versioned object from shared bucket
Put object in shared bucket (should be denied)
Delete object from shared bucket (should be denied)
Read from a different bucket (should be denied)
List a different bucket (should be denied)
Get versioned object from a different bucket (should be denied)
List all buckets in account (should be denied)
Get object tags from shared bucket — not in allowed actions (should be denied)

explanation:
The correct policy has three statements:

1. Allow s3:GetObject and s3:GetObjectVersion on arn:aws:s3:::shared-data-bucket/* for object-level access.
2. Allow s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::shared-data-bucket (bucket ARN without /*).
3. Explicit Deny for s3:ListAllMyBuckets on * prevents account enumeration.

All other actions are denied implicitly.

Common mistakes:
- Using wildcard Resource or Action for the Allow statements
- Forgetting the separate bucket-level ARN for ListBucket
- Omitting the explicit Deny for ListAllMyBuckets
- Conflating GetObjectVersion with GetObject (they are distinct IAM actions)

title: Handle a Traffic Spike
description: A 10x traffic spike is overwhelming your infrastructure. Select the correct scaling action for each metric.
scenario: Black Friday traffic has spiked 10x. Multiple services are hitting their limits. For each critical metric, choose the correct scaling action to stabilize the system.

options: Increase ASG max capacity to 50 and set target tracking to 60% CPU
Switch all instances to c5.4xlarge
Add a second ASG in a different region
Enable EC2 instance store caching
metrics.correctOption: Increase ASG max capacity to 50 and set target tracking to 60% CPU

options: Request concurrency limit increase and set reserved concurrency for critical functions
Reduce Lambda timeout to free up concurrency
Switch Lambda to ARM64 architecture
Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency for all functions
metrics.correctOption: Request concurrency limit increase and set reserved concurrency for critical functions

options: Switch to on-demand capacity mode for automatic scaling
Add a GSI to distribute writes
Enable DynamoDB Streams
Increase provisioned WCU to 80,000
metrics.correctOption: Switch to on-demand capacity mode for automatic scaling

options: Increase consumer Lambda batch size and concurrency
Switch to SQS FIFO queue
Increase message visibility timeout to 1 hour
Delete old messages from the queue
metrics.correctOption: Increase consumer Lambda batch size and concurrency

options: Request API Gateway account-level throttle increase via AWS Support
Switch from REST API to WebSocket API
Enable API Gateway caching
Add CloudFront in front of API Gateway
metrics.correctOption: Request API Gateway account-level throttle increase via AWS Support

metrics.targetValue: Reduce evictions below 30% without increasing cache misses
options: Scale up node type and enable cluster mode with auto-sharding
Flush all cache keys to start fresh
Increase TTL on all cached items to reduce churn
Switch from Redis to Memcached
metrics.correctOption: Scale up node type and enable cluster mode with auto-sharding

metrics.targetValue: Support 5x more concurrent application connections without changing RDS instance size
options: Enable RDS Proxy to pool and multiplex database connections
Restart RDS to clear stale connections
Set max_connections to 2000 in the parameter group
Switch to Aurora which has a higher default connection limit
metrics.correctOption: Enable RDS Proxy to pool and multiplex database connections

options: Enable CloudFront Origin Shield and increase origin response timeout
Increase CloudFront default TTL to reduce origin requests
Add a second ALB in a different region as failover origin
Disable CloudFront and route traffic directly to the ALB
metrics.correctOption: Enable CloudFront Origin Shield and increase origin response timeout

explanation:
The correct actions:

1. Increase ASG max capacity - the current limit prevents scaling out; target tracking at 60% CPU provides headroom.
2. Request Lambda concurrency increase via AWS Support, and set reserved concurrency to protect critical functions.
3. DynamoDB on-demand mode auto-scales without pre-provisioning.
4. Increasing Lambda batch size and concurrency for SQS consumers drains the queue faster.
5. API Gateway account-level throttle must be raised via Support - caching helps but doesn't solve a hard limit.
6. Scaling up ElastiCache nodes and enabling cluster mode distributes keyspace and reduces eviction pressure.
7. RDS Proxy pools persistent application connections and multiplexes them to RDS, allowing far more concurrent connections without resizing the instance.
8. CloudFront Origin Shield adds an extra caching layer between edge nodes and the origin; increasing origin timeout handles slow responses under spike load.

title: Investigate Production API Outage
description: Your production REST API is returning intermittent 500 errors during peak traffic. Investigate alerts, metrics, logs, and the incident timeline to identify the root cause and select the correct remediation actions.
scenario: At 14:00 UTC, your operations team received multiple alerts about API errors. The API is backed by API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB with provisioned capacity. Users are reporting timeouts and errors. Investigate the incident across all available signals and determine the root cause and correct response.

alerts.message: ThrottledRequests alarm: 112 throttled requests in the last 5 minutes on table 'orders'. Threshold: 0
5xx error rate alarm: 23% of requests returning 500 errors. Threshold: 2%
Duration alarm: Average execution time 12,400ms on function 'api-handler'. Threshold: 10,000ms
Error rate alarm: 8.2% invocation error rate on function 'api-handler'. Threshold: 5%
DynamoDB ConsumedReadCapacityUnits approaching provisioned limit on table 'orders'

logs.message: INIT cold start — runtime initialisation complete (540ms)
DynamoDB query failed after 3 retries — ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Table: orders
Task timed out after 29.00 seconds — pending DynamoDB GetItem on table 'orders'
DynamoDB query failed — ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Table: orders
Task timed out after 29.00 seconds — pending DynamoDB Query on table 'orders'
INIT cold start — runtime initialisation complete (620ms)
DynamoDB BatchGetItem throttled — ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. 23 unprocessed keys
502 Bad Gateway — upstream Lambda invocation failed (timeout)
Task timed out after 29.00 seconds — pending DynamoDB Scan on table 'orders'

timeline.event: Marketing campaign email sent to 50,000 subscribers with promotional code
API request rate begins increasing — up 40% from baseline
DynamoDB consumed read capacity reaches 95% of provisioned limit (95/100 RCU)
First DynamoDB ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors appear in Lambda logs
Lambda functions begin timing out waiting for throttled DynamoDB responses
CloudWatch info alert: DynamoDB capacity approaching limit
API Gateway 5xx rate alarm triggers — 23% error rate
Lambda error rate alarm triggers — SNS notification sent to ops team

actions.description: Switch DynamoDB 'orders' table to on-demand (PAY_PER_REQUEST) capacity mode
Enable DynamoDB auto-scaling with target utilisation of 70%
Add exponential backoff with jitter to Lambda DynamoDB calls
Enable API Gateway response caching for GET endpoints
Restart all Lambda function instances by updating the function configuration
Switch API Gateway to Regional endpoint type

answers.text: DynamoDB provisioned read capacity exceeded due to traffic spike from marketing campaign
Lambda cold starts causing cascading timeouts across the API
API Gateway throttling due to account-level usage plan limits
Lambda memory exhaustion causing out-of-memory crashes

explanation:
The root cause is DynamoDB throttling. The 'orders' table has fixed provisioned capacity of 100 RCU. When the marketing campaign drove a traffic spike at 14:00, read demand exceeded provisioned capacity within minutes. DynamoDB began returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors, causing Lambda functions to retry and eventually time out (29s). These timeouts cascaded to API Gateway, which returned 502/500 errors to clients.

Correct remediation actions:
1. Switch to on-demand capacity - immediately removes the throughput ceiling
2. If staying on provisioned, enable auto-scaling - prevents future capacity ceilings
3. Add exponential backoff with jitter - prevents retry storms that amplify throttling

Incorrect actions:
- Increasing Lambda memory won't help - the bottleneck is DynamoDB throttling, not Lambda compute
- API Gateway caching might reduce read load but doesn't fix the underlying capacity problem
- Restarting Lambda has no effect
- Changing endpoint type is irrelevant

title: Detect Infrastructure Drift
description: Your team uses Terraform to manage AWS infrastructure. After a colleague made emergency manual changes via the AWS Console, you need to identify which resources have drifted from the Terraform state.
scenario: During last week’s incident, a colleague made emergency changes via the AWS Console to restore service. Now you need to run a drift assessment before your next Terraform apply. Compare the expected Terraform state with the actual AWS configuration and identify which resources have drifted.
explanation:
Four resources have drifted from the Terraform state:

1. Security Group (sg-web-app) - Port 22 (SSH) was added manually for debugging during the incident. This is a security risk and should be removed, then the Terraform state updated if SSH access is needed.

2. RDS Instance (prod-db) - Instance class was upgraded from db.t3.medium to db.t3.large during the incident for more capacity. The Terraform configuration should be updated to reflect the new size if the upgrade is desired, or the instance should be downgraded.

3. IAM Role (lambda-execution-role) - AmazonS3FullAccess was attached manually. This violates least-privilege and should be replaced with a scoped policy granting only the specific S3 permissions needed.

4. Lambda Function (api-handler) - Memory was doubled (256→512MB), timeout increased (30→60s), and LOG_LEVEL changed from 'warn' to 'debug'. These were emergency changes to handle elevated load and improve debugging. The Terraform config should be updated to keep the memory increase if helpful, but LOG_LEVEL should revert to 'warn' for production.

title: Map On-Prem Services to AWS
description: Your organisation is migrating from on-premises infrastructure to AWS. Match each on-premises technology to the most appropriate AWS service equivalent for a lift-and-shift migration.
scenario: Your organisation is planning a lift-and-shift migration from on-premises data centres to AWS. For each on-premises technology currently in use, identify the most appropriate AWS managed service equivalent. Drag each on-prem technology to its matching AWS service.

pairs.definition: Amazon EC2 — Virtual servers with configurable instance types, auto-scaling groups, and placement groups for HA
Amazon EBS — Block-level storage volumes attached to EC2 instances with snapshots and encryption
Amazon RDS — Managed relational database with automated backups, Multi-AZ deployment, and read replicas
Amazon EFS — Fully managed elastic NFS file system for shared access across multiple EC2 instances
Elastic Load Balancing (ALB/NLB) — Distributes traffic across targets with health checks and SSL/TLS termination
Amazon CloudWatch — Metrics, alarms, logs, and dashboards for monitoring AWS resources and applications
Amazon SQS — Fully managed message queuing service with at-least-once delivery and dead-letter queues
AWS Directory Service — Managed Microsoft AD or Simple AD for user authentication and group policy management
AWS Backup — Centralised backup service with lifecycle policies, cross-region copy, and compliance reporting
Amazon Route 53 — Scalable DNS with health checks, failover routing, latency-based routing, and domain registration

explanation:
The key AWS service mappings for lift-and-shift migration:

• VMware VMs → EC2: Direct VM-to-instance migration using AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
• SAN storage → EBS: Block storage attached to instances; choose gp3 for general purpose, io2 for high IOPS
• PostgreSQL → RDS: Managed DB eliminates patching/backup overhead; use DMS for data migration
• NFS → EFS: Elastic shared file system with NFS v4 protocol compatibility
• F5 → ALB/NLB: ALB for HTTP/HTTPS (Layer 7), NLB for TCP/UDP (Layer 4)
• Nagios → CloudWatch: Native monitoring with custom metrics, alarms, and integration with SNS for alerting
• RabbitMQ → SQS: Managed queuing; consider Amazon MQ if AMQP protocol compatibility is required
• Active Directory → Directory Service: AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides full AD compatibility
• Veeam → AWS Backup: Centralised backup with retention policies and cross-account/cross-region support
• BIND DNS → Route 53: Managed DNS with 100% SLA and advanced routing policies

title: Execute DR Recovery Runbook
description: A catastrophic failure has occurred in your primary region (eu-west-1). Execute the disaster recovery runbook by filling in the missing parameters in each AWS CLI command to failover to the DR region (eu-west-2).
scenario: INCIDENT: eu-west-1 region is experiencing a major outage affecting multiple AZs. Your application stack includes Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB → ECS Fargate → RDS Aurora (with cross-region read replica in eu-west-2). Follow the DR runbook to failover all services to eu-west-2. Fill in the missing parameters for each command.

questions.template:
# Step 1: Promote the Aurora read replica to a standalone cluster
aws rds promote-read-replica-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier ___ \
  --region ___
questions.hint: The read replica cluster in the DR region needs to become a primary cluster

questions.template:
# Step 2: Update ECS service to scale up in DR region

questions.hint: Force CloudFront to fetch fresh content from the new DR origin

questions.template:
# Step 6: Notify the operations team
aws sns ___ \
  --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:123456789012:ops-notifications \
  --subject 'DR Failover Complete' \
  --message 'Failover to eu-west-2 completed. All services operational.'
questions.hint: Send a message to an SNS topic

explanation:
Disaster recovery failover procedure:

1. Promote Aurora read replica - The cross-region read replica becomes a standalone primary cluster in eu-west-2. For Aurora, use promote-read-replica-db-cluster (not promote-read-replica which is for non-Aurora RDS).

2. Scale ECS in DR - The DR cluster keeps a minimal task count (0 or 1) during normal operation. Scale to match primary (4 tasks) during failover.

3. Route 53 UPSERT - Updates the DNS alias record to point to the DR region's ALB. UPSERT is preferred over CREATE because it handles both new and existing records.

4. S3 sync - Copies only objects that are new or modified since the last cross-region replication. This catches any objects uploaded between the last replication and the outage.

5. CloudFront invalidation - Forces edge caches to fetch from the new origin (DR region). The path '/*' invalidates all cached content.

6. SNS publish - Sends a notification to the ops team confirming failover is complete. Critical for incident communication.

title: Fix Terraform S3 Security Config
description: Your security scanner has flagged several issues in a Terraform configuration for an S3 bucket storing application logs. Fix the configuration to meet compliance requirements: KMS encryption, versioning, no public access, and lifecycle rules.
scenario:
Your compliance team requires all S3 buckets storing application logs to meet these security standards:

1. Server-side encryption using AWS KMS (not AES256)
2. Versioning enabled for audit trail
3. All public access blocked
4. Lifecycle rule to transition objects to Glacier after 90 days

Fix the Terraform configuration to pass all checks.
explanation:
The Terraform configuration had four security issues:

1. Versioning Disabled → Enabled: Required for audit trail and accidental deletion protection. Without versioning, deleted or overwritten log files are unrecoverable.

2. AES256 → aws:kms: AES256 uses Amazon-managed keys with no audit trail. KMS provides key rotation, access policies, and CloudTrail logging of key usage - required for compliance.

3. restrict_public_buckets = false → true: This was the only public access block setting not enabled. Even if bucket policies don't grant public access today, this setting prevents any future policy from making the bucket public.

4. Missing lifecycle rule: Without a lifecycle configuration, logs accumulate indefinitely in Standard storage. Transitioning to Glacier after 90 days reduces storage costs by ~80% while maintaining compliance retention.

title: Detect IAM Privilege Escalation
description: Your security team detected suspicious IAM activity via GuardDuty. Analyse the CloudTrail logs to identify the attack chain and determine what type of attack was attempted.
scenario: GuardDuty has flagged high-severity findings related to IAM activity in your production account. The alerts triggered at 03:47 UTC from an unusual source IP. Examine the CloudTrail logs below to identify the attack chain, determine what the attacker accomplished, and select the correct classification of this attack.

logs.message: AssumeRole by arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-deploy-role from IP 10.0.1.55 — role session: github-actions-deploy-742
UpdateFunctionCode on function 'payment-processor' by role/ci-deploy-role — success
Query on table 'orders' by role/app-api-handler — 200 OK, 25 items returned
ListRoles by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — 200 OK, 34 roles returned
ListAttachedRolePolicies for role/lambda-admin-role by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — 200 OK
ListPolicies by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — 200 OK, 67 policies returned
CreatePolicy 'temp-escalation-policy' by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — policy grants iam:*, s3:*, lambda:*
AttachRolePolicy 'temp-escalation-policy' to role/lambda-admin-role by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — 200 OK
UpdateFunctionCode on function 'data-export' by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — function code replaced
Invoke function 'data-export' by user/dev-intern from IP 198.51.100.44 — 200 OK
Scan on table 'users' by role/app-api-handler — 200 OK, 150 items returned
HIGH severity finding: UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration — unusual API calls from IP 198.51.100.44
ListBuckets by role/app-api-handler — 200 OK (routine health check)

answers.text: IAM privilege escalation via policy attachment to Lambda execution role, followed by data exfiltration through modified Lambda function
S3 bucket data exfiltration via publicly exposed bucket policy
Compromised CI/CD pipeline credentials used to deploy malicious code
DDoS attack via excessive API calls causing Lambda throttling

explanation:
Attack chain analysis:

1. RECONNAISSANCE (03:41): The attacker (user/dev-intern from external IP 198.51.100.44) enumerated IAM roles and policies using ListRoles, ListAttachedRolePolicies, and ListPolicies. This revealed the existence of 'lambda-admin-role' with elevated privileges.

2. PRIVILEGE ESCALATION (03:43): The attacker created a custom policy ('temp-escalation-policy') granting iam:*, s3:*, and lambda:* permissions, then attached it to the 'lambda-admin-role'. The dev-intern user had iam:CreatePolicy and iam:AttachRolePolicy permissions - a dangerous combination that enables privilege escalation.

3. EXECUTION (03:44): The attacker modified the 'data-export' Lambda function's code (UpdateFunctionCode) and invoked it. The function now runs with the elevated 'lambda-admin-role' permissions.

4. DATA EXFILTRATION (03:44-03:46): The modified Lambda function, running with escalated privileges, accessed sensitive S3 objects: full-dump.csv (47MB) and customer-emails.csv (12MB) from the customer-data-prod bucket.

The CI/CD activity (03:12-03:25) from IP 10.0.1.55 is legitimate - different source IP, expected role, and normal deployment operations. The DynamoDB/S3 activity from app-api-handler (03:22, 03:49, 03:52) is routine application traffic.

Remediation: Revoke dev-intern's access, detach the malicious policy, restore the Lambda function code, rotate all credentials, and implement SCP guardrails preventing iam:CreatePolicy/AttachRolePolicy for developer users.

title: Review Architecture Security Flaws
description: You've been asked to review a colleague's architecture for a new serverless microservices application. Identify the security anti-patterns and select the correct fix for each issue.
scenario: A colleague has designed a serverless microservices architecture: API Gateway → 5 Lambda functions → DynamoDB + S3 + external payment API. You're conducting a security architecture review before the team begins implementation. Identify the anti-patterns and select the correct remediation for each.

issues.issue: All API endpoints are open with no authentication. The only access control is checking for an 'x-api-key' header in Lambda code.
options: Add CORS headers to all responses
Implement Cognito User Pool authorizer on API Gateway
Add WAF rules to block suspicious IPs
Rate-limit to 100 requests per minute
issues.correctOption: Implement Cognito User Pool authorizer on API Gateway

issues.issue: All 5 Lambda functions share one execution role with AdministratorAccess managed policy attached.
options: Add MFA requirement to the Lambda execution role
Create per-function roles with least-privilege permissions
Set Lambda concurrency limit to 10
Enable Lambda code signing
issues.correctOption: Create per-function roles with least-privilege permissions

issues.issue: Tables use default AWS-owned CMK for encryption. Data includes customer PII subject to GDPR.
options: Disable encryption for better write throughput
Enable DynamoDB Streams for change tracking
Switch to customer-managed KMS keys with automatic rotation
Add a GSI for faster PII lookups
issues.correctOption: Switch to customer-managed KMS keys with automatic rotation

issues.issue: Database credentials and API keys for the external payment service are stored as Lambda environment variables in plaintext.
options: Encrypt environment variables with Lambda's default KMS key
Store secrets in a private S3 bucket with bucket policy
Migrate to AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation and VPC endpoint access
Hardcode secrets in application code and use code signing
issues.correctOption: Migrate to AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation and VPC endpoint access

issues.issue: Payment processing Lambda calls an external payment API directly over the internet. No VPC configuration is used for any function.
options: Enable Lambda SnapStart for faster cold starts
Deploy payment Lambda in VPC with NAT Gateway for controlled outbound access
Add a security group to the Lambda function
Use API Gateway VPC Link
issues.correctOption: Deploy payment Lambda in VPC with NAT Gateway for controlled outbound access

issues.issue: Application logs contain unmasked customer email addresses, phone numbers, and partial credit card numbers for debugging.
options: Delete CloudWatch log groups after 24 hours
Restrict log access to administrators only
Implement log sanitisation in application code to mask PII before logging
Disable CloudWatch Logs and use print statements
issues.correctOption: Implement log sanitisation in application code to mask PII before logging

issues.issue: User-uploaded files are stored in S3 with a bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject from principal '*' for easy sharing.
options: Enable S3 versioning
Generate pre-signed URLs with expiration for authorised access
Add CloudFront in front of the bucket
Enable S3 Object Lock
issues.correctOption: Generate pre-signed URLs with expiration for authorised access

explanation:
Architecture security review findings:

1. Authentication at the edge: API keys in Lambda code provide no real security - they're shared secrets with no user identity. Cognito authorizers validate JWT tokens at the API Gateway level before code executes, providing user identity and token expiration.

2. Least-privilege IAM: AdministratorAccess on shared roles is the most dangerous anti-pattern. If one function is compromised, the attacker has full account access. Each function should have a dedicated role granting only the specific API actions and resources it needs.

3. Customer-managed KMS: While AWS-owned keys provide encryption, they offer no audit trail via CloudTrail, no key policy control, and no ability to disable/rotate keys independently. GDPR compliance typically requires demonstrable control over encryption keys.

4. Secrets Manager: Environment variables are visible in the Lambda console and API to anyone with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration. Secrets Manager provides encryption, automatic rotation, fine-grained IAM access control, and audit logging.

5. VPC + NAT: Running the payment Lambda in a VPC with NAT Gateway ensures outbound traffic goes through a controlled, monitored path. Security groups and NACLs provide additional network-level controls. VPC Flow Logs enable network traffic audit.

6. PII in logs: Compliance regulations (GDPR, PCI-DSS) prohibit storing unmasked PII in logs. Log sanitisation at the application layer masks sensitive data before it reaches CloudWatch, regardless of who has log access.

7. Public S3 access: principal '*' makes all objects publicly readable. Pre-signed URLs provide time-limited, per-object access that expires automatically, maintaining security while enabling sharing.

title: Recover From AZ Failure
description: Availability Zone eu-west-1a has experienced a complete failure. Your application is deployed across two AZs with Multi-AZ services. Order the correct recovery and validation steps to restore full service.
scenario: ALERT: AWS has confirmed an infrastructure failure in eu-west-1a. Your application is deployed in eu-west-1a and eu-west-1b behind an ALB with Auto Scaling, RDS Multi-AZ, and ElastiCache with replicas. Some services will auto-recover, but you need to follow the correct order to verify recovery, validate service health, and plan for resilience.

steps.text: Verify ALB health checks have automatically marked eu-west-1a targets as unhealthy and stopped routing traffic to them
Confirm Auto Scaling Group has detected unhealthy instances and is launching replacements in eu-west-1b
Verify RDS Multi-AZ automatic failover has promoted the standby instance in eu-west-1b to primary
Check ElastiCache replica in eu-west-1b has been promoted and application cache connections are restored
Run API smoke tests against production endpoints to validate end-to-end application health
Check CloudWatch dashboards for error rate, latency, and throughput metrics to confirm steady state
Update Route 53 health check thresholds if using DNS failover to accommodate single-AZ operation
Notify stakeholders with incident status, current capacity, and estimated time to full resilience
Plan and schedule capacity expansion into eu-west-1c to restore multi-AZ redundancy

explanation:
AZ failure recovery follows a verify → validate → communicate → plan sequence:

1-2. ALB + ASG verification: These are the fastest auto-recovery mechanisms. ALB health checks detect failures within seconds, and ASG launches replacements within minutes. Verify these are working before checking database layer.

3-4. Data tier failover: RDS Multi-AZ failover typically completes in 60-120 seconds. ElastiCache automatic failover depends on configuration but should complete within minutes. Verify these before running end-to-end tests.

5-6. Validation: Smoke tests verify the full request path works. CloudWatch metrics confirm stable operation - look for error rates returning to baseline, latency normalising, and throughput recovering. Don't skip this - auto-recovery succeeding doesn't mean the application is fully healthy.

7. Route 53 adjustment: If using health-check-based failover, the thresholds may need temporary adjustment since you're running at reduced capacity in a single AZ.

8. Communication: Only notify stakeholders after you have confirmed facts - current health, remaining capacity, and whether manual intervention is needed.

9. Resilience planning: Don't wait for eu-west-1a to recover - plan capacity in eu-west-1c so you're not single-AZ for an extended period. This is non-urgent but should be scheduled.

title: Tune RDS Database Performance
description: Your Aurora MySQL database is experiencing slow query performance under load. The DBA has identified parameter group settings that need tuning. Configure the correct values for each setting.
scenario: Your Aurora MySQL database (db.r6g.xlarge, 32GB RAM) is experiencing slow query performance during peak hours. After running Performance Insights, the DBA identified several parameter group settings that need adjustment. Configure each parameter to its optimal value.
explanation:
Optimal parameter tuning for Aurora MySQL db.r6g.xlarge (32GB RAM):

1. innodb_buffer_pool_size → 20GB (21474836480): The buffer pool should be approximately 60-75% of total instance memory. At 128MB (default), the database constantly reads from disk. 20GB allows most active data to reside in memory, dramatically reducing I/O.

2. max_connections → 200: 50 connections is far too low for production workloads. With connection pooling, 200 provides adequate headroom. Setting to 1000 wastes memory (each connection consumes ~10MB) and risks resource exhaustion.

3. slow_query_log → 1 (enabled): Essential for identifying performance bottlenecks. Without this, you're blind to which queries are slow. Combine with Performance Insights for query-level analysis.

4. long_query_time → 2 seconds: Captures queries taking more than 2 seconds. The default of 10 seconds misses many problematic queries. 1 second may log too many routine queries in high-throughput systems.

5. query_cache_type → 0 (disabled): The MySQL query cache is deprecated and removed in MySQL 8.0. Even in 5.7, it causes mutex contention under concurrent writes. Disable it - use application-level caching (ElastiCache) instead.

6. innodb_io_capacity → 2000: This tells InnoDB how many IOPS the storage can handle. Aurora's storage can deliver thousands of IOPS; the default of 200 (designed for spinning disks) artificially throttles background I/O operations like flushing dirty pages and merge operations.

title: Build Serverless Data Pipeline
description: Design a serverless event-driven data pipeline on AWS. Users upload CSV files which must be processed, transformed, stored in a database, and trigger a notification on completion.
scenario:
Your team needs to build an event-driven data processing pipeline. The flow:

1. Users upload CSV files to S3
2. The upload triggers a Lambda function
3. The function sends a message to SQS for reliable processing
4. A consumer Lambda reads from SQS and transforms the data
5. Transformed data is stored in DynamoDB
6. An SNS notification is sent when processing completes

Design this pipeline by placing components and connecting them in the correct order.
validationChecks: S3 upload bucket is connected to a Lambda trigger function
File trigger Lambda sends messages to SQS for decoupled processing
SQS queue feeds the transform Lambda for reliable message consumption
Transform Lambda writes processed data to DynamoDB
Transform Lambda publishes completion notification to SNS
No unnecessary components are placed (e.g. EC2, CloudFront, API Gateway)
explanation:
This serverless pipeline uses event-driven architecture with loose coupling:

1. S3 → Lambda (Event Notification): S3 event notifications trigger the file trigger Lambda on every ObjectCreated event. This is an async push model - no polling needed.

2. Lambda → SQS: Rather than processing the file directly, the trigger Lambda sends a message to SQS. This decouples file detection from processing, provides retry capability, and handles bursts via SQS's built-in buffering.

3. SQS → Lambda (Event Source Mapping): The transform Lambda uses SQS as an event source. Lambda automatically polls SQS, manages batch size, and handles failures with configurable retry and dead-letter queue.

4. Lambda → DynamoDB: The transform Lambda parses CSV data and writes structured records to DynamoDB. NoSQL is ideal here - schema flexibility handles varying CSV formats, and DynamoDB scales automatically.

5. Lambda → SNS: After successful processing, the Lambda publishes to SNS. Subscribers (email, webhook, other Lambdas) receive the notification. This enables the pipeline to trigger downstream processes without tight coupling.

Why not the other components?
- API Gateway: No direct user API needed - uploads go straight to S3 (via presigned URLs)
- CloudFront: Not needed for a data processing pipeline
- EC2: Unnecessary - Lambda handles the compute without server management
- Kinesis: Overkill for file processing - better suited for continuous real-time streaming
- Step Functions: Useful for complex multi-step workflows but overkill here - the SQS decoupling achieves the same reliability
- RDS: Not needed - DynamoDB provides the right data model for processed records

title: Label a VPC Architecture
description: A VPC architecture diagram has been prepared for a 3-tier application. Identify each component by selecting the correct label from the dropdown menus placed on the diagram.
scenario: You're onboarding onto a team that manages a 3-tier application on AWS. The lead engineer has drawn the VPC architecture but left the labels blank as a knowledge check. Identify every component on the diagram: the gateway connecting the VPC to the internet, the subnet types, the role of each EC2 instance, the networking device enabling private subnet internet access, the database service, and the default route for each route table.

NAT Gateway

hotspots.label: Managed relational database, Multi-AZ
Public subnet routes internet traffic via IGW
Private subnet routes internet traffic via NAT

explanation:
VPC architecture components:

• Internet Gateway (IGW): The only component that connects a VPC directly to the internet. It’s horizontally scaled, redundant, and HA by default. Not to be confused with NAT Gateway (outbound-only) or Virtual Private Gateway (VPN/Direct Connect).

• Public vs Private Subnets: A subnet is "public" if its route table has a route to an IGW (0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxxx). A "private" subnet has no such route - it can only access the internet outbound via a NAT Gateway.

• Bastion Host: An EC2 instance in the public subnet used as an SSH jump box to reach instances in private subnets. It has an Elastic IP and strict security group rules (SSH from known IPs only).

• NAT Gateway: Sits in the public subnet and allows instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections (e.g. software updates, API calls) without being directly reachable from the internet. Requires an Elastic IP.

• Application Server: Runs in the private subnet with no public IP. Accessible only from the bastion host via SSH or from the load balancer. This isolation is a security best practice.

• Amazon RDS (MySQL): Managed relational database in the private subnet with Multi-AZ for high availability. Never placed in a public subnet in production.

• Route Tables: The public route table needs 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxxx so instances can reach the internet directly. The private route table needs 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx so outbound traffic goes through the NAT Gateway. Both route tables automatically include 10.0.0.0/16 → local for intra-VPC traffic.

title: Wire Up EC2 Network Access
description: You’ve been handed a VPC with EC2 instances, an RDS database, and networking components already provisioned — but none of the security groups or route tables are configured. Set up the correct rules to enable secure access.
scenario: Configure the security groups and route tables for this VPC. Your office IP range is 203.0.113.0/24. Wrong choices represent common misconfigurations that would either break access or create security vulnerabilities.

configItems.label: App Server SG — Inbound SSH (22) Source
options: sg-bastion

configItems.label: App Server SG — Inbound Application Port
Database SG — Inbound MySQL (3306) Source
options: sg-app-server
sg-bastion

configItems.label: Public Route Table — 0.0.0.0/0 Target
options: igw-xxxx
nat-xxxx
vgw-xxxx
local

configItems.label: Private Route Table — 0.0.0.0/0 Target
options: igw-xxxx
nat-xxxx
vgw-xxxx
pcx-xxxx

explanation:
Security group and route table configuration explained:

1. Bastion SSH Source → 203.0.113.0/24: Never open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 (the entire internet). Restrict to your office IP range. Using 10.0.0.0/16 would allow any VPC instance to SSH in, which is too broad. 10.0.1.0/24 would only allow the subnet itself.

2. Bastion Inbound Port → 22: Port 22 is SSH (Linux). Port 3389 is RDP (Windows). Port 443 is HTTPS and port 80 is HTTP - neither is for remote shell access.

3. App Server SSH Source → sg-bastion: Referencing a security group (not an IP) is the AWS best practice. It allows any instance in the bastion SG to connect, even if IPs change. Using 10.0.1.10/32 would work but is fragile - if the bastion IP changes, access breaks. Never use 0.0.0.0/0 for private subnet SSH.

4. App Server Port → 8080: The application runs on port 8080. Port 80/443 would only work if a reverse proxy is configured. Port 3000 is for Node.js development servers, not production.

5. Database Source → sg-app-server: Only the application server should access the database. Using 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database to the internet (critical vulnerability). Using sg-bastion would allow the bastion to connect directly, bypassing the application layer. 10.0.0.0/16 is too broad.

6. Database Port → 3306: MySQL uses port 3306. Port 5432 is PostgreSQL, 1433 is SQL Server, and 27017 is MongoDB. Using the wrong port means the app server can’t reach the database.

7. Public RT Target → igw-xxxx: Public subnets need a route to the Internet Gateway for direct internet access. Routing to NAT is for private subnets. Routing to VPN Gateway (vgw) is for hybrid connectivity. "local" only allows VPC-internal traffic.

8. Private RT Target → nat-xxxx: Private subnets route outbound internet traffic through the NAT Gateway. Routing to IGW would make the subnet effectively public (security risk). VPN Gateway is for on-premises connectivity.
